title: Cyclic Subspace (Krylov Space)
content: Defines the T-cyclic subspace generated by v as the K-span of the orbit {T^0 v, T^1 v, T^2 v, ...}. Uses Set.range over ℕ-indexed powers of T as a Module.End K V. This is the Krylov space in numerical linear algebra and the cyclic submodule in algebra. In finite dimensions, this subspace has dimension equal to the degree of the minimal polynomial of T restricted to v.
mathContext:
$$\text{cyc}(T, v) = \text{span}_K\{v, Tv, T^2v, \ldots\} = \text{span}_K\{T^k v : k \in \mathbb{N}\}$$
This is the smallest $T$-invariant $K$-subspace containing $v$. In module language: the $K[X]$-submodule of $V$ generated by $v$ under the action $X \cdot v = T(v)$.
significance: The Krylov space is fundamental to both theoretical (module structure theorem, rational canonical form) and computational (Krylov subspace methods, Lanczos, GMRES) linear algebra. The generalization from finite to infinite dimensions is natural: the definition works unchanged for any Module.End K V without assuming finite dimensionality.

title: Evaluation Map φᵥ : K[X] → V
content: Defines the K-linear evaluation map φᵥ(p) = p(T)(v): the ring homomorphism aeval T applied pointwise to v. This is the fundamental bridge between polynomial algebra and geometric structure: its image is the cyclic subspace (range_evalMap_eq_cyclicSubspace) and its kernel is the annihilator ideal {p : p(T)v = 0}. The K-linearity proof requires showing aeval T is compatible with addition (map_add) and scalar multiplication (using toLinearMap.map_smul).
mathContext:
$$\varphi_v : K[X] \to V, \quad p \mapsto p(T)(v) = (\text{aeval}_T\, p)(v)$$
This is K-linear. Kernel: $\ker(\varphi_v) = \{p \in K[X] : p(T)v = 0\}$ = annihilator ideal.
Image: $\text{im}(\varphi_v) = \text{cyc}(T, v)$.
The first isomorphism theorem gives: $V \cong K[X]/\ker(\varphi_v)$ when $v$ is cyclic.
significance: The evaluation map is the algebraic formulation of the cyclic structure: V is a cyclic K[X]-module via the action p * v = p(T)v, and φᵥ is the K[X]-module map K[X] → V sending 1 to v. Its surjectivity characterizes v as a cyclic vector. The kernel structure connects to the minimal polynomial theory.

title: Cyclic Subspace is T-Invariant
content: Proves that T maps the cyclic subspace into itself: T(cyc(T,v)) ⊆ cyc(T,v). The proof uses Submodule.map_le_iff_le_comap to convert the map condition to a comap condition, then Submodule.span_le to reduce to generators. For each generator T^k v, T(T^k v) = T^(k+1) v is shown via pow_succ' and definitional unfolding, then pow_mem_cyclicSubspace establishes the membership.
mathContext:
$$T(\text{cyc}(T,v)) \subseteq \text{cyc}(T,v)$$
Proof: $T(T^k v) = T^{k+1} v \in \text{cyc}(T,v)$. The map $\texttt{Submodule.map T}$ sends span to span, and the image generators $T \cdot T^k v = T^{k+1} v$ are themselves generators of cyc$(T,v)$.
significance: T-invariance is the foundational property of cyclic subspaces. In module theory, it means cyc(T,v) is a K[X]-submodule of V (not just a K-subspace). This property is implicitly assumed in all applications — without it, the K[X]-module quotient V/cyc(T,v) would not be well-defined as a module.

title: Image of Evaluation Map = Cyclic Subspace
content: The fundamental structural theorem: LinearMap.range (evalMap T v) = cyclicSubspace T v. Forward direction: given p(T)v in the range, induct on p using Polynomial.induction_on' — monomials aeval_monomial show a·T^n v ∈ cyc(T,v), and polynomial addition uses Submodule.add_mem. Backward direction: span induction shows each T^k v is in the range (φᵥ(X^k) = T^k v by evalMap_X_pow), then close under K-linearity.
mathContext:
$$\text{im}(\varphi_v) = \text{cyc}(T, v)$$
The key identity: $\varphi_v(X^k) = (\text{aeval}_T X^k)(v) = (T^k)(v)$. So generators $T^k v$ of cyc$(T,v)$ are exactly the values of $\varphi_v$ on monomials.

Proof by `Polynomial.induction_on'`: basis = monomials, step = addition.
significance: This theorem formally establishes the equivalence between the geometric (Krylov vectors) and algebraic (K[X]-module quotient) descriptions of cyclic subspaces. It is the key lemma that makes the module-theoretic approach work: once we know the image is exactly the cyclic subspace, the theory of K[X]-modules applies directly.

title: Cyclic Vector ↔ Surjective Evaluation Map
content: Proves v is cyclic for T (generates all of V) iff the evaluation map φᵥ is surjective. The proof is a one-line rewrite: IsCyclicVector unfolds to cyclicSubspace = ⊤, range_evalMap_eq_cyclicSubspace shows this equals range(φᵥ) = ⊤, and LinearMap.range_eq_top states this is equivalent to surjectivity.
mathContext:
$$\text{IsCyclicVector}(T, v) \iff \text{im}(\varphi_v) = V \iff \varphi_v \text{ surjective}$$
Equivalently: $v$ generates $V$ as a $K[X]$-module.

When $V = K^n$: $v$ is cyclic iff the Krylov matrix $[v, Tv, \ldots, T^{n-1}v]$ is invertible.
significance: The surjectivity characterization is the algebraic foundation for all subsequent results about cyclic vectors. It converts geometric questions (does {T^k v} span V?) into algebraic ones (is φᵥ : K[X] → V surjective?), unlocking the first isomorphism theorem K[X]/ann(v) ≅ V and connecting to ideal theory.

title: Annihilator is Closed Under Multiplication
content: If p(T)v = 0, then (q·p)(T)v = 0 for any q. The proof is a two-step rewrite: map_mul on aeval T shows aeval T (q*p) = (aeval T q) * (aeval T p), then LinearMap.mul_apply applies (aeval T q) to (aeval T p)(v) = 0, and map_zero finishes. This establishes that the annihilator {p : p(T)v = 0} is a K[X]-ideal (closed under multiplication by any polynomial).
mathContext:
$$(q \cdot p)(T)(v) = q(T)(p(T)(v)) = q(T)(0) = 0$$
This shows $\text{ann}(v) = \{p \in K[X] : p(T)v = 0\}$ is an ideal: if $p \in \text{ann}(v)$, then $qp \in \text{ann}(v)$ for all $q \in K[X]$.
significance: The ideal structure of the annihilator is what makes the module-theoretic approach powerful. As K[X] is a PID, every ideal is principal, so ann(v) = (μ) for some polynomial μ — the minimal polynomial of T relative to v. This connects the abstract ideal theory to the concrete minimal polynomial.

title: Orbit Bounded by Minimal Polynomial Degree
content: For an integral T, proves that T^k v lies in span{v, Tv, ..., T^(d-1)v} for all k ≥ d = deg(minpoly K T). The proof has two parts: (1) Base case k=d: from minpoly(T)(v) = 0 and the monic leading coefficient, extract T^d v = -(sum of lower T^i v), showing T^d v ∈ W. (2) T-invariance of W: by induction on generators, T(T^i v) = T^(i+1) v uses boundary case T^d v ∈ W and lower cases by index. (3) Main: induction on k ≥ d.
mathContext:
$$\text{If } T^d v \in \text{span}\{v, Tv, \ldots, T^{d-1}v\}, \text{ then } T^k v \in \text{span}\{v, \ldots, T^{d-1}v\} \text{ for all } k \geq d$$
From $\mu_T(T)(v) = 0$ (monic, degree $d$): $T^d v = -(a_0 v + a_1 Tv + \ldots + a_{d-1} T^{d-1}v)$.

This shows: $\dim_K(\text{cyc}(T,v)) \leq \deg(\mu_T)$.
significance: This is the key finiteness theorem: even without assuming finite-dimensional V, the cyclic subspace of any vector is at most deg(minpoly T)-dimensional when T is integral. Combined with the lower bound from the evaluation map, this gives dim(cyc(T,v)) = deg(minpoly T) for cyclic vectors — the module-theoretic content of the structure theorem.

title: Matrix Nonderogatory → Module Cyclic
content: For infinite fields K and n > 0, proves that a matrix M with IsNonderogatoryMatrix (minpoly K M = charpoly M) has a cyclic vector in the sense of IsCyclicVectorMatrix. This bridges the finite-dimensional matrix theory (CayleyHamiltonMinpolyOQ05OQ01.lean) and the module-theoretic framework. The proof delegates entirely to NonderogatoryComplete.nonderogatory_has_cyclic_vector from the parent file.
mathContext:
$$\text{minpoly}_K(M) = \text{charpoly}(M) \implies \exists v,\, \text{IsCyclicVector}(M, v)$$
Over infinite fields, the nonderogatory condition (minpoly = charpoly) implies the existence of cyclic vectors. The proof uses union avoidance: the finitely many proper invariant subspaces defined by irreducible factors don't cover all of $K^n$ when $K$ is infinite.
significance: This theorem connects the two different perspectives on nonderogatory operators. The finite-dimensional (matrix) definition uses charpoly which doesn't generalize; the module-theoretic definition uses cyclic K[X]-modules which does. This theorem shows the two agree in the overlapping domain (finite dimensions, infinite field).

title: Minimal Polynomial Has Minimal Degree
content: For finite-dimensional V and integral T, proves no nonzero polynomial of smaller degree than minpoly K T can annihilate T. If p annihilates T (aeval T p = 0) and p ≠ 0, then minpoly K T divides p (minpoly.dvd), so deg(minpoly) ≤ deg(p) by natDegree_le_of_dvd. This contradicts p.natDegree < (minpoly K T).natDegree, so no such p exists.
mathContext:
$$p \neq 0,\, \deg(p) < \deg(\mu_T) \implies p(T) \neq 0$$
Proof: $p(T) = 0 \implies \mu_T \mid p$ (by `minpoly.dvd`) $\implies \deg(\mu_T) \leq \deg(p)$, contradiction.

This is the minimality part of 'minimal polynomial': $\mu_T$ is the unique monic annihilating polynomial of least degree.
significance: This theorem formalizes the defining property of the minimal polynomial. It is used implicitly throughout the theory: when we say 'minpoly is in the annihilator', this theorem ensures it's the generator. The proof is a clean application of minpoly.dvd — the Mathlib lemma that states minpoly divides any annihilating polynomial.
